name_en: Xiao Chi Gan (Small Red Tangerine Pu-erh)
processing: As with other tangerine pu-erh, a small tangerine is hollowed out, stuffed with ripe pu-erh and dried in the sun or at low heat. The name seems to point to a riper, red-skinned fruit than that of Xiao Qing Gan.
harvest_season: Depends on the fruit: tangerine pu-erh goes from green fruit in August to fully red in December, and a red tangerine would belong to the later end.
appearance_dry: A small, round, dried tangerine shell, reddish to dark brown, packed with dark tea.
appearance_wet: Softened peel over dark brown ripe pu-erh leaf.
taste_profile: Typical of red-peel tangerine pu-erh, warm sweet citrus and honey sit over an earthy ripe base, softer and less sharp than the green fruit version.

brewing.notes: Rinse quickly, then brew the fruit whole for a slow release or break off pieces of peel for more citrus.

vintage_note: Tangerine pu-erh is usually sold by the year it was made, often in tins of individually wrapped fruit. Little is documented on this particular name, so ask which fruit and peel stage it uses, and whether the tangerine truly comes from Xinhui, which is the most valued origin for the peel.
description:
Xiao Chi Gan means 'small red tangerine': a little fruit, hollowed and stuffed with ripe pu-erh. The name is far less documented than its green cousin Xiao Qing Gan, and it seems to be used for a riper-fruit version, not a formally defined type.

Tangerine pu-erh in general is made by cutting the top from the fruit, removing the pulp, packing the shell with ripe tea and drying it, ideally in the sun. As the fruit ripens its peel loses sharp oils and gains sugar, so a red peel gives a rounder result than a green one.

Expect warm, honeyed citrus over earthy ripe tea, with less zest than the green fruit. Use boiling water and a quick rinse. Brewing the whole fruit gives a slow, long session; breaking the peel gives stronger citrus sooner.

When buying, the label matters less than the fruit. Xinhui in Guangdong is the most valued peel origin, but the term itself does not guarantee it, so ask the seller. Try one next to a Xiao Qing Gan to see what the ripening of the fruit changes.
history: Little is documented about when this particular name came into use. It belongs to the wider family of Xinhui tangerine and ripe pu-erh teas, in which the peel stages are sorted as green, semi-red and fully red.
